messages.author: 20758fda448fdbda
messages.subject: Explicitly modeling correlation properly?
parts:
I thought I understood this, and now I am having second thoughts. I have a vector of data to which I want to fit a gamma distribution. As the gamma's parameters are very strongly correlated, I want to compare an implicit vs. explicit correlation structure. My thought was that model 1 should have priors directly on alpha and beta, and model two should have a multivariate normal which generates correlated alpha and beta which are then used. Is this proper? Are the versions of the two models I have below correct?

Thank you.

Implicit:

data {
  int<lower = 0> N;
  vector<lower = 0.0>[N] Y;
}
parameters {
  real<lower = 0.0> alpha;
  real<lower = 0.0> beta;
}
model {
  alpha ~ uniform(0.0, 1000.0);
  beta ~ uniform(0.0, 1000.0);
  Y ~ gamma(alpha, beta);
}
generated quantities {
  real<lower = 0.0> Y_post;
  vector[N] PointLikelihoods;
  for (i in 1:N) {
    PointLikelihoods[i] <- exp(gamma_log(Y[i], alpha, beta));
  }
  Y_post <- gamma_rng(alpha, beta);
}


Explicit:

data {
  int<lower = 0> N;
  vector<lower = 0.0>[N] Y;
}
parameters {
  vector[2] Pars;
  vector[2] mu;                      // multivariate normal (MVN) prior mean: implied (0,0)
  corr_matrix[2] Sigma_corr;         // MVN prior correlation
  vector<lower = 0.0>[2] Sigma_scale;  // MVN prior sd scale for covariance: implied (0,0)
}
transformed parameters {
  real<lower = 0.0> alpha;           // prior for alpha
  real<lower = 0.0> beta;            // prior for beta
  alpha <- exp(Pars[1]);             // ensure non-negativity
  beta <- exp(Pars[2]);              // ensure non-negativity
}
model {
  matrix[2, 2] Sigma;                // will become MVN prior covariance
  Sigma_corr ~ lkj_corr(4.0);        // prior on correlation (mode is identity)
  Sigma <- diag_matrix(Sigma_scale) * cholesky_decompose(Sigma_corr);  // scale cor to cov
  Pars ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu, Sigma);
  Y ~ gamma(alpha, beta);
}
generated quantities {
  real<lower = 0.0> Y_post;
  vector[N] PointLikelihoods;
  for (i in 1:N) {
    PointLikelihoods[i] <- exp(gamma_log(Y[i], alpha, beta));
  }
  Y_post <- gamma_rng(alpha, beta);
}

messages.author: d0b8e6084efd456d
messages.subject: Re: Explicitly modeling correlation properly?
parts:
Hi Avraham, 

just a quick note. You 'scale cor to cov' with:
diag_matrix(Sigma_scale) * cholesky_decompose(Sigma_corr)

Wouldn't you rather:
diag_matrix(Sigma_scale) * Sigma_corr * diag_matrix(Sigma_scale)

messages.author: d0b8e6084efd456d
messages.subject: Re: Explicitly modeling correlation properly?
parts:
I might be a little confused, but I think that this "trick" only works for diagonal matrices. 

As, to stay with Ben's answer it would suggest that
cholesky_decompose(  diag_matrix(sdTheta[k]) * RhoTheta[k] * diag_matrix(sdTheta[k]) );
is simply 
diag_matrix(sdTheta[k]) * cholesky_decompose(RhoTheta[k]);

In other words, if
SigmaTheta[k]=diag_matrix(sdTheta[k]) * RhoTheta[k] * diag_matrix(sdTheta[k])
This would impliy that
cholesky_decompose( SigmaTheta[k] ) = diag_matrix(sdTheta[k]) * cholesky_decompose(RhoTheta[k]);
which infact is not true if SigmaTheta is not diagonal, ie., if SigmaThetas off-diagonal elements are not zero.

  for (i in 1:N) {

parts:
Why not just break the correlation between shape (alpha) and rate (beta) parameters by parameterising the gamma distribution in terms of mean (alpha/beta) and variation (alpha/beta^2)? Then in the transformed parameters block set alpha = mean^2 / variation and beta = mean / variation. I haven't tried this myself, but it's similar to the trick suggested in the stan manual for parameterizing the beta distribution (I believe in terms of mean and dispersion rather than shape parameters alpha and beta). I'd be interested to hear if this works for the gamma distribution as well. You might want to try different types of priors for the mean and the variance (or sd), and check how they translate in terms of alpha and beta, and compare to your current uniform priors (0,1000) for alpha and beta.

Luc

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Explicitly modeling correlation properly?
parts:
On Saturday, March 29, 2014 8:48:42 PM UTC-4, Avraham Adler wrote:
If you note my original post, I fixed the name.

And Dr. Goodrich, I apologize profusely for not originally ascribing credit properly.

Not a big deal. The real credit should go to Lewandowski, Kurowicka, and Joe but Bob and I have long since given up on being able to spell all that (hence the LKJ).

Anyway, the broader point here is that calculating a matrix decomposition of a parameterized matrix in Stan is expensive, in part because the number of operations depends on the cube of the number of rows and in part because Stan has to use its auto-diff mechanism to compute the derivatives (which involves a chain rule whose number of links also depends on the cube of the number of rows) with respect to each scalar parameter. So if you do something like

cholesky_decompose( diag_matrix(scales) * correlation_matrix * diag_matrix(scales) )

or

cholesky decompose( variance * correlation matrix )

the cholesky_decompose() function just sees a square matrix and does not recognize that these are equivalent to

diag_matrix(scales) * cholesky_decompose(correlation_matrix)

and

sqrt(variance) * choleksy_decompose(correlation_matrix)

respectively (although as Philippe pointed out, this particular trick only applies with a diagonal matrix or a scalar).

However, you ultimately want something equivalent which does not entail taking an expensive Cholesky decomposition of a correlation matrix. The attachment constructs and L such that L * L' is a correlation matrix that is distributed LKJ with shape parameter eta. So, if you use that, then the above expressions are equivalent to

diag_matrix(scales) * L

and

sqrt(variance) * L

But wait, there's more! If something is getting a multivariate normal prior (or more generally anything in the elliptical distribution family), then you don't want to actually use of the multi_normal functions (ideally, those should only be used for likelihoods of data). You can make Pars a local or transformed parameter that is a function of the primitive parameter vector z via the multivariate Matt trick:

z ~ normal(0,1);

This way avoids having to solve a triangular system of equations inside one of the multi_normal functions. All that said, none of this makes much difference when dealing with a 2x2 covariance matrix, but it is much better when the dimension of the covariance matrix is large.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Explicitly modeling correlation properly?
parts:
On Mar 30, 2014, at 6:07 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> On Saturday, March 29, 2014 8:48:42 PM UTC-4, Avraham Adler wrote:

I think Ben's being too modest here. He figured out both how to implement
the LKJ model using matrix operations and how to use it for applied
modeling. See:

http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/Visualization.pdf

which has nice comparisons to (inverse) Wishart. It's changed the way
we think about modeling covariance matrices --- instead of scaled (inverse)
Wisharts, as recommended in Andrew's books, we now favor a scaled
correlation matrix with an LKJ prior. Too bad Andrew couldn't have snuck
it into the 3rd Edition of Bayesian Data Analysis --- it'll definitely be
in the 2nd Edition of Gelman and Hill :-)

- Bob

Michael Betancourt has a paper forthcoming with Mark Girolami
where they analyze the "centered" parameterizations in a univariate
setting for HMC (I don't think they did multivariate), and like others in
the previous literature for Metropolis and Gibbs, found that how effective
it is depends on the amount of data. The reparameterization is most
effective with less data.

It looks similar to the manual as far as I can see.

>> cholesky_decompose( diag_matrix(scales) * correlation_matrix * diag_matrix(scales) )
>>
>> or
>>
>> cholesky decompose( variance * correlation matrix )
>>
>> the cholesky_decompose() function just sees a square matrix and does not recognize that these are equivalent to
>>
>> diag_matrix(scales) * cholesky_decompose(correlation_matrix)
>>
>> and
>>
>> sqrt(variance) * choleksy_decompose(correlation_matrix)
>>
>> respectively (although as Philippe pointed out, this particular trick only applies with a diagonal matrix or a scalar).
>>
>> However, you ultimately want something equivalent which does not entail taking an expensive Cholesky decomposition of a correlation matrix. The attachment constructs and L such that L * L' is a correlation matrix that is distributed LKJ with shape parameter eta. So, if you use that, then the above expressions are equivalent to
>>
>> diag_matrix(scales) * L
>>
>> and
>>
>> sqrt(variance) * L
>>
>> But wait, there's more! If something is getting a multivariate normal prior (or more generally anything in the elliptical distribution family), then you don't want to actually use of the multi_normal functions (ideally, those should only be used for likelihoods of data). You can make Pars a local or transformed parameter that is a function of the primitive parameter vector z via the multivariate Matt trick:
>>
>> z ~ normal(0,1);
>>
>> This way avoids having to solve a triangular system of equations inside one of the multi_normal functions. All that said, none of this makes much difference when dealing with a 2x2 covariance matrix, but it is much better when the dimension of the covariance matrix is large.
>>
>> Ben

That is correct.  

In these simple hierarchies, tau -> theta -> y, the centered and non-centered parameterizations
just shift around the correlations to either tau -> theta or theta -> y.  If you have lots of data then theta -> y is
highly constrained and we want to break that correlation by using a centered parameterization.  If you have little
data then tau -> theta is highly constrained and we want to break that correlation by using a non-centered
parameterization.  To get an intuition as to why these “break” the correlations see Figure 4.

Of course if you have more than the tree layers then there are many more possible parameterizations
and things become more challenging.
